8n35vs:199: In current agent research, memory/skill management follows three routes: (1) manual curation (e.g., Anthropic Skills), which requires heavy human expert involvement and cannot scale; (2) heuristic methods, which rely on fixed rules and lack downstream performance feedback; (3) short-horizon RL adaptation, which focuses only on in-task skill operations and cannot handle complex management operations such as skill updates and deletions. SkillOS fills the gap in the third route—through task grouping and composite rewards, it enables the curator to learn skill-management decisions over long time horizons.
960xkw:279: The paper trains the curator with GRPO (Grouped Reward Policy Optimization) and finds that dropping the KL divergence term actually aids policy exploration. This finding has important engineering implications: the KL term is typically introduced to limit the policy update magnitude and prevent catastrophic forgetting, but in curation scenarios, excessive conservatism can prevent the curator from learning bold delete and update operations. The curator needs to explore various combinations of insert/update/delete, and even attempt “destructive” operations to understand the boundaries of the skill repository. This exploratory freedom is critical to learning an effective long-term curation policy. In practice, teams that require more conservative curation behavior can consider adding the KL term in the later training stages for fine-tuning, rather than constraining it throughout.
